questions.prompt: A branch scale was away for repair for two weeks, and every handout of those two weeks has no weight. Parcels were counted as usual. Which description fits the missing weights?
options: Missing because of the weight itself: heavy handouts were not recorded
Missing at random given branch and date, both of which are recorded
Not missing: a blank weight means the handout weighed nothing
Missing completely at random across all branches and dates
questions.explanation: The blanks are explained by two recorded fields, the branch and the date; within that branch and fortnight nothing about the weight decided whether it was recorded.
misconceptions: Assumes every gap depends on the hidden value; here the cause is a known date range at one branch
Reads a blank as a zero, which would lower every average of weight
Ignores that the blanks sit in one branch and one fortnight, which the data show

questions.prompt: An online form offers household sizes 1 to 6. Larger households leave the field blank. An analyst computes the mean household size from the rows where it is recorded. What happens to that mean?
options: It is too low, because the blanks are the large households
It is unbiased, because 82% of the rows are still there
It is too high, because small households answer less often
It is unbiased but less precise, as with any missing data
questions.explanation: The value itself decides whether it is missing (above 6 cannot be entered), so the recorded sizes are a selection of the small ones and their mean is too low.
misconceptions: Believes a large share of observed rows guarantees a fair picture, whatever the reason for the blanks
Reverses the mechanism: the form stops the large households from answering, not the small ones
Treats every gap as completely at random, where only precision is lost

questions.prompt: Eligibility is income per member at most 1,000 SAR. An audit finds that a few households just above the line reported one or two members more than they have. What does this do to "parcels per eligible household"?
options: Nothing: a few wrong sizes average out over thousands of households
It raises the figure, because larger households receive more parcels
It lowers the figure: households counted as eligible that receive almost nothing enter the denominator
It cannot be known without auditing every household
questions.explanation: Over-reporting moves ineligible households into the denominator; they collect few parcels, so the average per eligible household falls.
misconceptions: Expects errors to cancel, which holds for random error and not for error in one direction at a threshold
Follows the reported size to the parcels, although the branch desk hands out by the family card, not by the register
Believes direction needs a census; the mechanism alone gives the direction, and a sample gives the size

questions.prompt: Clerks sometimes mistype a household size by one, up as often as down, for any household. Which statement is right?
options: The mean size is roughly unchanged, but households near the eligibility line are misclassified in both directions
The mean size rises, because larger numbers have more digits to mistype
Nothing changes: symmetric errors cancel in every statistic
The data must be discarded: any error makes the estimate meaningless
questions.explanation: Random error leaves averages about right but adds noise to any yes-or-no rule at a threshold, which usually weakens differences between groups.
misconceptions: Invents a direction for an error that is symmetric by description
Extends cancelling in a mean to a threshold rule, where each error can flip a household
Treats all error as fatal instead of asking how far it moves the result

questions.prompt: One branch uploaded no log file for nine days in August. The households it serves show fewer parcels in the quarter than their neighbours. What is the right reading?
options: Those households were under-served in August
Their figure is biased downwards by rows that are missing, and no field imputation repairs it
Impute the mean number of parcels for the blank cells of those days
The gap is completely at random, so only precision is lost
questions.explanation: Whole rows are missing for a known branch and period: the count for its districts is too low, and the remedy is to ask the owner for the file or to report the gap beside the figure.
misconceptions: Takes missing rows for missing service; the handouts may have happened and never reached a file
Looks for blank cells to fill; there are none, because whole rows are absent
Ignores that the gap sits in one branch and so lowers the figure of its districts in particular

questions.prompt: An open table describes the year 2022, was published on 15 March 2023, and you downloaded it on 2 October 2026. Which date is the refresh date of your provenance record?
options: 2022, the year the data describe
15 March 2023, the day of publication
2 October 2026, the day your copy was taken
Today, since the file is still on the portal
questions.explanation: The refresh date is the day your copy was taken; the reference year goes into coverage and the gap between them into limits.
misconceptions: Confuses the reference period, which belongs in coverage, with the age of the copy
Takes the release date of the publisher for the day the copy was taken
Assumes the copy follows the portal; a downloaded file does not update itself

questions.prompt: Which owner field lets a stranger act on a provenance record a year from now?
options: "IT"
"Widad"
"See the shared drive"
"Registration supervisor (Widad Al-Ghunaim); extracts approved by the data protection officer"
questions.explanation: An owner is a role that will still exist when the person has moved on, with the name of who holds it now and who approves access.
misconceptions: Names a department that cannot answer what a column means
Uses a first name that means nothing to a reader outside the team
Points to a place, not to a person or role who answers for the data

questions.prompt: You hold a register extract approved for "service coverage analysis, Q3 2026". A colleague asks you to use it to build a contact list for a fundraising campaign. What is the right step?
options: Use it: the extract is already on your computer
Ask the data protection officer: the approval names another purpose
Use it after removing the national ID numbers
Refuse: an extract can never be used twice
questions.explanation: The sharing basis names a purpose; a new purpose is a new decision by whoever approved the sharing, not by the analyst who holds the file.
misconceptions: Treats possession as permission
Believes dropping one identifier changes the purpose the data were shared for
Turns a purpose limit into an absolute ban; a new approval may be given

questions.prompt: Which line belongs in the limits field of the record of the branch logs?
options: "A week can be uploaded twice or be missing, and no file says so"
"The logs are in 14 files"
"Hazem Al-Sulaim uploads them weekly"
"The data are messy"
questions.explanation: A limit is a specific thing the data cannot be trusted for, stated so that the next analyst can test for it.
misconceptions: Describes the form of the extract, which belongs in origin
Names the owner and the routine, not what the data cannot be trusted for
States a mood, not a fact a reader can check or plan around

questions.prompt: A district shows 118% coverage: more registered households than the 2022 survey estimates as low-income. What goes into the report?
options: The register holds fabricated households in that district
The coverage is capped at 100% to keep the table tidy
The frame is a 2022 estimate and the district has grown; coverage ratios are approximate
The district is dropped from the analysis
questions.explanation: A ratio above one tells you about the age and error of the frame, and that caveat applies to every district, not only to the one where it shows.
misconceptions: Reads the ratio as a fact about the numerator when the denominator is the old estimate
Hides the evidence that the frame is out of date
Removes real households because an outside estimate is imperfect

questions.prompt: You join 209,620 log rows to the register on household_id with a left join and get 210,585 rows. No error was raised. What happened?
options: Some log rows had no household in the register
The join found households that the logs had missed
Rounding in the row counter
Some household ids are in the register more than once, so their handouts were repeated
questions.explanation: A left join returns more rows than its left table only when a key matches several rows on the right: the register is not one row per id.
misconceptions: Expects unmatched rows to add rows; in a left join they stay one row each
Believes a join can discover records; it only repeats or matches the rows it is given
Treats a whole-row difference as noise

questions.prompt: Which line makes the join itself fail when the register has a repeated household_id?
options: logs.merge(reg, on="household_id", how="left")
logs.merge(reg, on="household_id", how="left", validate="many_to_one")
logs.merge(reg, on="household_id", how="inner")
logs.merge(reg, on="household_id", how="left").drop_duplicates()
questions.explanation: validate="many_to_one" checks that the key is unique in the right table and raises an error before any row is produced.
misconceptions: Assumes a left join protects the row count; it does not check the right table
Believes an inner join removes duplicates; it repeats them just the same
Removes exact copies afterwards, but the repeated rows differ in the register columns

questions.prompt: After key repair, 421 log rows carry a household id that is not in the register. What do you do with them?
options: Drop them silently: they cannot be analysed
Assign them to the household with the most similar id
Set them aside in a file with the reason, and count them in the join log
Keep them in the joined table with blank household fields
questions.explanation: Rows in must equal rows out plus rows set aside; each set-aside row keeps its reason so the owner can repair the source.
misconceptions: Loses rows without a trace, so the counts no longer add up
Invents a link; a wrong household then gains parcels it never received
Lets rows without a household flow into every later average and group

questions.prompt: You match walk-in records to the register by name. At a low threshold you find more matches, and more of them are wrong. A false match gives one family the handouts of another. Which threshold do you choose?
options: The lowest: more matches means more complete data
The one with the highest total number of matches on the labelled pairs
The one a colleague used on another dataset
One where false matches on labelled pairs are rare, accepting some missed matches for manual review
questions.explanation: The two errors do not cost the same: a missed match can be reviewed by hand, a false match silently corrupts two households.
misconceptions: Counts matches without asking whether they are right
Optimises volume, where the cost of a false match is what matters
Assumes a threshold transfers between datasets with different names and typing habits

questions.prompt: Household ids are "H" and six digits. Some log rows hold "h482913", " H482913 " or "H-482913". Which repair is safe?
options: Strip spaces, upper-case and remove the hyphen, then check the result against the pattern
Replace each odd id by the nearest valid id in the register
Leave them: the join will ignore them
Delete the rows, since hand-typed ids cannot be trusted
questions.explanation: A repair is safe when the rule cannot change which household is meant: case, spaces and a hyphen carry no information; "nearest id" does.
misconceptions: Changes which household a row belongs to on the strength of similarity alone
Accepts losing rows that a rule can repair with certainty
Discards rows whose meaning is unambiguous

questions.prompt: A rule says "log_id never repeats". Which quality dimension does it test?
options: Completeness
Validity
Uniqueness
Timeliness
questions.explanation: Uniqueness rules say that a key identifies one row; a week uploaded twice breaks exactly this rule.
misconceptions: Confuses "every row is there once" with "no value is blank"
Takes any rule about a column for a rule about its allowed values
Picks a dimension that concerns when data arrive, not whether rows repeat

questions.prompt: A rebuild stops with the message "AssertionError". Which message would let a branch supervisor fix the source?
options: "Validation failed in 3 checks"
"Row 2,214 is invalid"
"B05: 377 handouts weigh 21 to 32 kg per parcel; the standard is 9 to 15. Was the weight entered in pounds?"
"weight_kg check returned False"
questions.explanation: A readable failure names the rule in plain words, the owner of the rows, how many rows and an example, so the person who can fix the source knows what to look at.
misconceptions: Counts failures without saying where or what
Points to a row number of your table, which means nothing in the file of the branch
Names the column but not the branch, the values or the likely cause

questions.prompt: Every column of a batch passes its own rule: dates are dates, parcels are 1 to 3, weights are 5 to 50. Yet 30 handouts are dated before the household registered. Which kind of rule catches them?
options: A stricter range on handout_date
A rule across two fields: handout_date on or after registered_on
A uniqueness rule on log_id
No rule can: the values are all valid
questions.explanation: Some faults are invisible in any single column; consistency rules compare fields with each other, or one source with another.
misconceptions: Tightens one column when the fault only exists between two
Applies a rule about repeated rows to a fault of logic
Believes validity of each column is all a rule can express

questions.prompt: Why do the rules run on every rebuild and not once, when the dataset is first made?
options: Because the sources change: a branch can change its export next month
Because rules slow the build, and a slow build is a careful one
Because the first run of a rule is unreliable
Because auditors count how many times rules were run
questions.explanation: A rule protects the next build from a change nobody announced; a rule that ran once only describes the past.
misconceptions: Mistakes cost for value
Believes repetition makes a deterministic check more accurate
Treats rules as paperwork rather than as protection of the next answer

questions.prompt: You wrote a rule "weight_kg between 5 and 50" and it reports 4,000 failures on a build you believe is clean. What do you check first?
options: Delete the rule: it is clearly too strict
Widen the range until nothing fails
Set the rule to a warning and move on
The failing rows and their branches: a real fault and a wrong rule look the same until you read examples
questions.explanation: A suite must pass on a clean build and fail on a corrupted one; when it fails, examples by owner tell you whether the data or the rule is wrong.
misconceptions: Removes the alarm instead of finding out what it rang for
Fits the rule to the data, so it can never fail again
Keeps a rule nobody will read

questions.prompt: Household size is missing for 18% of households, mostly large ones, and large households receive more parcels per visit. You drop the rows with no size. What happens to "parcels per eligible household"?
options: It is unchanged: dropping rows only shrinks the sample
It rises, because fewer households share the parcels
It falls, because the households that receive most were removed
It becomes undefined
questions.explanation: Complete-case analysis assumes the dropped households are like the rest; here they are larger and receive more, so the average of those left is too low.
misconceptions: Assumes the dropped households resemble the kept ones
Forgets that the parcels of the dropped households leave the numerator too
Believes any missing value prevents an estimate

questions.prompt: You replace every missing household size by the median, 5. The missing households are mostly of size 7 or more. What is the main cost?
options: Nothing: the median is robust
Large households are classified with a size of 5, so some truly eligible ones are counted as ineligible
The median changes each time the code runs
The dataset grows by 18%
questions.explanation: A single value puts every missing household in the middle; a rule that depends on the size then misclassifies exactly the households the gap hides.
misconceptions: Mistakes robustness to outliers for correctness of an imputed value
Thinks a median is random
Confuses filling a field with adding rows

questions.prompt: Branches hand out 1, 2 or 3 parcels per visit according to the family card. Which imputation of a missing household size uses that?
options: The overall mean size, 5.3
A size drawn at random between 1 and 14
Zero, to be conservative
The typical size of households that receive the same number of parcels per visit
questions.explanation: An imputation should use what is observed and related to the missing value; parcels per visit carries information about the size.
misconceptions: Ignores every observed fact about the household
Adds noise unrelated to the household
Uses an impossible value, and "conservative" has no direction here

questions.prompt: Your best estimate is 2.06 parcels per eligible household per month. Under defensible assumptions about the missing sizes it ranges from 2.02 to 2.07, and the standard is 2.0. What do you report for the network as a whole?
options: 2.06, without the range: one number is clearer
"About 2.06 (2.02 to 2.07 under different assumptions about missing sizes): at or above the standard"
"Unknown", because 18% of sizes are missing
2.07, the most favourable value
questions.explanation: When the whole range sits on one side of the decision line, say so and show the range; the reader sees both the estimate and how far it can move.
misconceptions: Hides how much depends on an assumption
Lets missing data veto a conclusion the whole range supports
Chooses the assumption by the answer it gives

questions.prompt: A district is at 1.97 under one imputation and 2.02 under another; the standard is 2.0. How does it appear in the report?
options: Below the standard: 1.97 is the cautious figure
At the standard: 2.02 rounds to 2
As "cannot be classified with these data", with both values
It is left out of the table
questions.explanation: A district whose side of the line depends on the method is reported as undecided, with the values, so that nobody acts on an artefact of imputation.
misconceptions: Picks one assumption and presents it as the finding
Picks the other assumption for the same reason
Removes exactly the district where the uncertainty matters

questions.prompt: A colleague replaces national ID numbers by their SHA-256 hash and calls the table anonymous. Someone holds a list of 40,000 ID numbers of residents. What can they do?
options: Nothing: a hash cannot be reversed
Hash their list and look each value up in the table
Only identify people whose number begins with the same digit
Decrypt the hashes with the SHA-256 key
questions.explanation: A plain hash is the same for everyone who computes it; anyone with candidate identifiers can recompute and match them.
misconceptions: Stops at "one-way" and misses that the same input always gives the same output
Imagines a partial weakness where the match is exact
Thinks a plain hash has a key

questions.prompt: What makes a keyed hash (HMAC) hold where a plain hash fails?
options: It is longer
It uses a newer algorithm
It cannot be recomputed without a key that is kept apart from the data
It changes every time it is computed
questions.explanation: The pseudonym depends on a secret; whoever lacks the key cannot test candidates, and the key is the additional information that must be kept separately.
misconceptions: Attributes safety to output length
Looks for safety in the algorithm rather than in the secret
Confuses a keyed hash with a random token; a pseudonym must be stable to link records

questions.prompt: A table holds a keyed pseudonym, the district, the exact registration date and the household size. Is it still personal data?
options: No: there is no name and no ID number in it
No: a keyed hash is anonymisation
Only if the key is lost
Yes: pseudonymised data remain personal, and the other fields together can single a household out
questions.explanation: Pseudonymised data can still be linked to a person with additional information, and a rare combination of ordinary fields can identify a household without any key.
misconceptions: Equates personal data with direct identifiers
Confuses pseudonymisation with anonymisation
Reverses the role of the key: its existence is what keeps re-identification possible

questions.prompt: Which repository shows that a dataset is rebuildable?
options: One that contains the final CSV and a notebook with saved outputs
One with a README describing each manual step in order
One whose single command turns the raw files into the dataset, its join log and its rule results
One with the raw personal data committed for convenience
questions.explanation: Rebuildable means a command, not a description: the same raw files give the same dataset, with the counts and rule results produced by the run itself.
misconceptions: Shows a result, not a way to produce it again
Relies on a person repeating steps exactly
Publishes personal data in the name of reproducibility

questions.prompt: The question is "parcels per eligible household per month, by district". Which set of register fields do you request?
options: Every field: unused columns can be dropped later
household_id, district_id, registered_on, status, household_size, monthly_income_sar
household_id and district_id only: everything else is personal
national_id, head_name and district_id, to be sure who is who
questions.explanation: Each requested field has a step of the answer that needs it: the link, the group, the population and the eligibility rule; names and ID numbers have none.
misconceptions: Collects first and justifies never
Removes fields the answer cannot be computed without
Takes direct identifiers that no step of the answer uses

questions.prompt: A branch file holds dates such as 03/07/2026 and 11/04/2026. How do you decide whether the day or the month comes first?
options: Let the library guess each value
Assume day first: it is the local habit
Look at all values of that branch: a first part above 12 anywhere settles it for the whole file
Drop every date whose two parts are both 12 or less
questions.explanation: The layout is a property of the source: one unambiguous value in the file decides for all, and the decision is logged per branch.
misconceptions: Accepts a per-value guess that can read one file both ways
Replaces evidence by habit; two branches use donated software with month first
Discards over a third of the rows for want of looking at the others

questions.prompt: A cursor API states no total. You made 12 requests; each sent the cursor that the answer before returned, the last answer's next cursor is null, and the 4,410 records received have 4,410 distinct ids. What does the source inventory say?
options: Complete beyond doubt, since the chain is unbroken and ends in a null cursor
Incomplete, since a source that states no total can never be read in full
Complete as far as the chain shows; one count from elsewhere would prove it
Unknown until every record is compared by hand with the source system itself
questions.explanation: Three checks pass: the chain, the end and the keys. The fourth, the count, needs a figure from somewhere else, such as a count endpoint or a daily summary from the owner, so the inventory states what was proved and what is still open.
misconceptions: Takes three checks for four: a chain can be unbroken and still start after records the service never served
Believes completeness needs a stated total, when a count from a second route can stand in for it
Asks for a manual comparison when one independent count would settle the question

questions.prompt: A nightly ingestion calls an API of a partner organisation. Which answer should the job retry with a growing wait, rather than stop at once and raise an alert?
options: 400 Bad Request: the query string has a field the API does not know
401 Unauthorized: the access token expired during the night
404 Not Found: the endpoint was renamed in a new version
429 Too Many Requests: the service asks the job to wait 30 seconds
questions.explanation: A 429 says the service is limiting requests for now; waiting at least as long as it asks and trying again can succeed. The other three give the same answer however often they are asked, so the job stops and a person is alerted.
misconceptions: Retries a malformed request, which fails the same way every time
Expects an expired token to become valid by waiting; it needs a person or a renewal step
Treats a missing endpoint as a busy one; asking again cannot find it

questions.prompt: A match links three records of one household: the register (2022, size 4, phone ending 314), a walk-in form (April 2026, size 6, phone ending 902) and a home visit (October 2026, size 5, no phone). The rules: a verified value beats a reported one, the most recent phone wins, and a blank never wins. Which master record follows?
options: Size 5 from the home visit, and the phone ending 902 from the walk-in form
Size 6 and phone ending 902: the walk-in form is the newest complete record
Size 4 and phone ending 314: the register is the system of record
Size 5 from the visit and no phone, since the visit is the newest record of all
questions.explanation: Each field is decided on its own: the size verified at the visit beats the reported sizes, and the most recent phone given is on the walk-in form, because the visit recorded none and a blank never wins.
misconceptions: Keeps one whole record, so a reported size overrides the verified one
Trusts the oldest system for every field, keeping a size and a phone that are out of date
Lets the newest record win every field, so its blank phone erases a known number

questions.prompt: A survey samples 900 households. 540 answer by phone and 300 of them say yes. A random 1 in 3 of the 360 nonrespondents are visited at home; 100 of the 120 visited answer and 30 say yes. What is the two-phase estimate of the share that says yes?
options: 55.6%: the phone answers, since the visits were only a sample
51.6%: all 640 answers pooled, each counted once
43.3%: each visited answer counts three times, the subsampling rate
45.3%: each visited answer stands for 3.6 nonrespondents
questions.explanation: The 100 visited answers stand for all 360 nonrespondents, 3.6 each: (300 + 3.6 × 30) ÷ 900 = 45.3%. This assumes the 20 visited households that still did not answer are like the 100 that did.
misconceptions: Assumes nonrespondents answer like respondents, which the follow-up exists to test
Pools answers from two phases with different sampling rates as if each stood for one household
Weights by the share visited and forgets the 20 visited households that still did not answer

questions.prompt: Two monthly series changed their question in July, each with a three-month overlap in which both versions were asked. Series A: new-to-old ratios 0.81, 0.80 and 0.82, alike at the desk and by phone. Series B: ratios 0.92, 0.74 and 0.61. What do you do?
options: Link both, each with the mean ratio of its overlap: 0.81 and 0.76
Link A with its factor; report B as two series with a marked break
Link neither: any change of wording ends a series for good
Link B only, since its larger ratios show the stronger effect of the change
questions.explanation: A ratio that holds across months and groups lets one factor put the old series on the new basis. B's ratio drifts by 0.31 in three months, so no single factor is right for its past: the series breaks.
misconceptions: Averages a drifting ratio as if it were noise around one factor
Gives up a stable overlap that was collected to make the link possible
Reads the size of the ratio, not its stability, as the reason to link
